extracted.intended_audience: Catholic faithful / catechism students / parishioners preparing for sacraments
extracted.subtask_description: Question-and-answer catechetical guidance on the Catholic sacraments (Mass/Eucharist, Extreme Unction, Holy Orders, Matrimony) explaining their nature, requirements, proper reception, and related practices. Intended as instructional rules and norms for lay Catholics and those preparing for sacraments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four ends/kinds of sacrifice
rubrics_metrics.description: The early people offered four kinds of sacrifice: one for sin, another in thanksgiving for benefits received, another as an act of worship, and another to beg God's blessing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four ends or objects are the purposes for which the one Christian sacrifice of the holy Mass is offered. (Also referenced: the fruits/benefits of Mass are divided into four classes: to the priest, to the one for whom Mass is offered, to those present, and to all the faithful.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass is the same sacrifice as the Cross
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mass is the same sacrifice as that of the Cross because the offering and the priest are the same—Christ Our Blessed Lord—and the ends for which the sacrifice of the Mass is offered are the same as those of the sacrifice of the Cross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the Cross the offering was the body and blood of Our Lord; the one who offered it was Our Lord; the reason was to atone for sin; the one to whom He offered it was the heavenly Father. At Mass the object offered is Our Lord's body and blood, offered by Our Lord Himself through the priest, for sin, and to the heavenly Father. All things are the same except the blood is not shed and Christ does not die again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eucharist is both a sacrifice and a Sacrament
rubrics_metrics.description: The Holy Eucharist is both a sacrifice (when offered at Mass) and a Sacrament (when received or reserved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Sacrament has three necessary things: (1) the outward sign—appearance of bread and wine; (2) the inward grace—Jesus Christ Himself, the Author and Dispenser of graces; (3) instituted by Our Lord. At Mass the body and blood are consecrated separately and kept separate to signify Christ's death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials required for Mass Eucharist
rubrics_metrics.description: The bread and wine used at Mass must be of a particular kind: wheaten bread and wine of the grape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this requirement the priest began to buy the bread and wine and the people gave money for his support rather than bringing gifts of uncertain suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of simony (buying sacred things or blessings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Money given to the priest for Mass is not to pay for the Mass; to buy a holy thing for money is simony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paying only for the material of religious articles is allowed; buying a blessing or trying to buy sacred things is simony (named after Simon who tried to bribe the Apostles).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to assist at Mass (behavioural standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assist at Mass with great interior recollection and piety and with every outward mark of respect and devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not show indifference or disrespect (no idle talking, no looking around). Keep eyes fixed on Our Lord present on the altar as if admitted into the presence of a king. Failure to show respect is displeasing and may be punished by God; some offer prayers and Communions in reparation for insults to the Blessed Sacrament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best manner of hearing Mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer the Mass to God with the priest for the same purpose for which it is said, meditate on Christ's sufferings and death, and go to Holy Communion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically offer it for the priest's intention (for the dead, conversion of sinners, good of others), especially for worship, thanksgiving, atonement, and to obtain graces. Prepare for Communion if in a state of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of receiving Holy Communion (norms and recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church requires reception of Holy Communion at least once a year, but faithful should receive more often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All good Catholics should go to Holy Communion at least once a week on Sunday; those wishing to lead truly holy lives should receive more often or even daily. When unable to receive, one may make a spiritual Communion (an earnest desire, preparation, imagination of reception, and thanksgiving).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiritual Communion practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A spiritual Communion is an earnest desire to receive Communion when one cannot receive sacramentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare as if really going to Communion, imagine receiving and returning, then give thanks as you would if you had received. This is an act of devotion pleasing to God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four classes of fruits/benefits of Mass
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Holy Mass is offered, the fruits or benefits are divided into four classes: (1) to the priest who celebrates, (2) to the one for whom he offers the Mass, (3) to those present, (4) to all the faithful throughout the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme Unction (definition & scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme Unction (Last Anointing) is the Sacrament which, through the anointing and prayer of the priest, gives health and strength to the soul and sometimes to the body when one is in danger of death from sickness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is a separate and distinct Sacrament using oil as a sign of strength. It is administered generally after confession and receiving Viaticum, and is intended in a special way for the body as well as the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may receive Extreme Unction (timing & cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme Unction must be given only in sickness—when one is in danger of death from sickness, wound, or accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should not be delayed until extreme danger; if possible, receive it while one has the use of the senses. It may be received more than once if in danger of death multiple times. Danger from external causes (battle, shipwreck, fire) does not ordinarily permit anointing unless fear causes internal danger (e.g., death from fright). If in doubt, send for the priest and let him judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of Extreme Unction
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects: (1) comfort in sickness and strength against temptation; (2) remission of venial sins and cleansing from remains of sin; (3) restoration to health when God sees fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remains of sin refer to inclinations and bad habits remaining after sins are forgiven; the Sacrament helps remove the ease and inclination to sin acquired by habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition for receiving Extreme Unction
rubrics_metrics.description: One should receive Extreme Unction in a state of grace and with lively faith and resignation to the will of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is generally given after confession and Viaticum; if the sick person has been neglectful of religion, send for the priest even if he refuses, and let the priest judge and act. Do not delay out of fear that the sacrament will hasten death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical preparations for home administration of sacraments
rubrics_metrics.description: When the priest comes to administer the sacraments at home, prepare: a small table covered with a clean white cloth, a crucifix, one or two lighted candles in candlesticks, holy water with a sprinkler, a glass of clean water, a tablespoon, a napkin for under the chin, and a piece of white cotton wadding if requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optionally have water, towel, and a piece of bread or lemon for purifying the priest's fingers. Families should keep these things ready to avoid disrespectful administration or delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful reception of Blessed Sacrament and processions
rubrics_metrics.description: Receive Our Lord with all possible respect when He comes to visit the house; meeting the priest at the door with a lighted candle and going before him to the sickroom is a praiseworthy practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Catholic countries the priest may bring the Blessed Sacrament vested and in procession; the Church would like such solemn processions whenever the Blessed Sacrament is carried from place to place, but may limit outward display in streets where non-Catholics might insult the Blessed Sacrament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy Orders defined and minister
rubrics_metrics.description: Holy Orders is the Sacrament by which bishops, priests, and other ministers (deacons, subdeacons) are ordained and receive the power and grace to perform sacred duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only bishops can confer Holy Orders (cardinals who are bishops and the Pope as Bishop of Rome can also confer). The sequence of clerical advancement described: tonsure, Minor Orders, subdeacon, deacon, priest, bishop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements to receive Holy Orders worthily
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive Holy Orders worthily it is necessary to be in the state of grace, to have the necessary knowledge, and a divine call to this sacred office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Knowledge' means having learned what a priest should know; 'divine call' refers to vocation—an interior calling from God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and powers of ordained ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordained ministers can perform the duties of any office to which they have been ordained, but not those above their order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a subdeacon cannot take the place of a deacon; a deacon cannot act as a priest; but a priest may perform duties of deacon or subdeacon because he has been ordained to those offices. Nuns, sisters, and brothers are not ministers because they have not received Holy Orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Mass (ceremonial forms) and equivalence of value
rubrics_metrics.description: There are different kinds of Mass as to ceremonies: Low Mass (no display), High Mass / Missa Cantata (sung by priest and choir), and Solemn High Mass (three ministers and full ceremonies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All kinds of Mass are alike in spiritual value. Masses said in black vestments are Requiem Masses for the repose of the dead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vespers attendance guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Vespers is a portion of the Divine Office sung on Sunday afternoon or evening and usually followed by Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not a mortal sin to stay from Vespers on Sundays, because there is no law obliging attendance, but good Catholics will attend when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrimony as a Sacrament and who may validly receive it
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sacrament of Matrimony unites a Christian man and woman in lawful marriage; non-Christians do not receive the grace of the Sacrament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Christian couple cannot be united in lawful marriage in any other way than by the Sacrament, because Christ raised marriage to the dignity of a Sacrament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawfulness and indissolubility of Christian marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: The bond of Christian marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Church may permit spouses to separate for good reason, they remain married. Some marriages may be declared null if an impediment existed at the time of ceremony rendering the marriage invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impediments to marriage and required disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Couples should privately inform the priest of any circumstance that might be an impediment: whether both are Christians/Catholics; prior solemn engagements; vows to chastity or religious life; degrees of consanguinity; whether one was ever godparent to the other's child; prior marriages and proof of death of former spouse; intention to marry; lawful age; health; residence and parish status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give at least three weeks' notice before marriage except in special necessity. Do not finalize invitations until arrangements with the pastor are made, as impediments may delay or nullify marriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of marrying under false beliefs about impediments (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a woman, believing her first husband to be dead, marries another man and the first husband returns alive, the second marriage is invalid (no marriage) because the first husband was still living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Church will require the woman to leave the second man and return to her lawful husband once the truth is known.
